    19	| Edit existing document | Unpack → edit XML → repack - see Editing Existing Documents below |
    20	
    21	### Converting .doc to .docx
    22	
    23	Legacy `.doc` files must be converted before editing:
    24	
    25	```bash
    26	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx document.doc
    27	```
    28	
    29	### Reading Content
    30	
    31	```bash
    32	# Text extraction with tracked changes
    33	pandoc --track-changes=all document.docx -o output.md
    34	
    35	# Raw XML access
    36	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
    37	```
    38	
    39	### Converting to Images
    40	
    41	```bash
    42	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf document.docx
    43	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 document.pdf page
    44	```
    45	
    46	### Accepting Tracked Changes
    47	
    48	To produce a clean document with all tracked changes accepted (requires LibreOffice):
    49	
    50	```bash
    51	python scripts/accept_changes.py input.docx output.docx
    52	```
    53	
    54	---
    55	
    56	## Creating New Documents
    57	
    58	Generate .docx files with JavaScript, then validate. Install: `npm install -g docx`
    59	
    60	### Setup
    61	```javascript
    62	const { Document, Packer, Paragraph, TextRun, Table, TableRow, TableCell, ImageRun,
    63	        Header, Footer, AlignmentType, PageOrientation, LevelFormat, ExternalHyperlink,
    64	        InternalHyperlink, Bookmark, FootnoteReferenceRun, PositionalTab,
    65	        PositionalTabAlignment, PositionalTabRelativeTo, PositionalTabLeader,
    66	        TabStopType, TabStopPosition, Column, SectionType,
    67	        TableOfContents, HeadingLevel, BorderStyle, WidthType, ShadingType,
    68	        VerticalAlign, PageNumber, PageBreak } = require('docx');
    69	
    70	const doc = new Document({ sections: [{ children: [/* content */] }] });
    71	Packer.toBuffer(doc).then(buffer => fs.writeFileSync("doc.docx", buffer));
    72	```
    73	
    74	### Validation
    75	After creating the file, validate it. If validation fails, unpack, fix the XML, and repack.
    76	```bash
    77	python scripts/office/validate.py doc.docx
    78	```
    79	
    80	### Page Size
    81	
    82	```javascript
    83	// CRITICAL: docx-js defaults to A4, not US Letter
    84	// Always set page size explicitly for consistent results
    85	sections: [{
    86	  properties: {
    87	    page: {
    88	      size: {
    89	        width: 12240,   // 8.5 inches in DXA
    90	        height: 15840   // 11 inches in DXA
    91	      },
    92	      margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 } // 1 inch margins
    93	    }
    94	  },
    95	  children: [/* content */]
    96	}]
    97	```
    98	
    99	**Common page sizes (DXA units, 1440 DXA = 1 inch):**
   100	
   101	| Paper | Width | Height | Content Width (1" margins) |
   102	|-------|-------|--------|---------------------------|
   103	| US Letter | 12,240 | 15,840 | 9,360 |
   104	| A4 (default) | 11,906 | 16,838 | 9,026 |
   105	
   106	**Landscape orientation:** docx-js swaps width/height internally, so pass portrait dimensions and let it handle the swap:
   107	```javascript
   108	size: {
   109	  width: 12240,   // Pass SHORT edge as width
   110	  height: 15840,  // Pass LONG edge as height
   111	  orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE  // docx-js swaps them in the XML
   112	},
   113	// Content width = 15840 - left margin - right margin (uses the long edge)
   114	```
   115	
   116	### Styles (Override Built-in Headings)
   117	
   118	Use Arial as the default font (universally supported). Keep titles black for readability.
   119	
   120	```javascript
   121	const doc = new Document({
   122	  styles: {
   123	    default: { document: { run: { font: "Arial", size: 24 } } }, // 12pt default
   124	    paragraphStyles: [
   125	      // IMPORTANT: Use exact IDs to override built-in styles
   126	      { id: "Heading1", name: "Heading 1", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   127	        run: { size: 32, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   128	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 240, after: 240 }, outlineLevel: 0 } }, // outlineLevel required for TOC
   129	      { id: "Heading2", name: "Heading 2", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   130	        run: { size: 28, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   131	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 180, after: 180 }, outlineLevel: 1 } },
   132	    ]
   133	  },
   134	  sections: [{
   135	    children: [
   136	      new Paragraph({ heading: HeadingLevel.HEADING_1, children: [new TextRun("Title")] }),
   137	    ]
   138	  }]
   139	});
   140	```
   141	
   142	### Lists (NEVER use unicode bullets)
   143	
   144	```javascript
   145	// ❌ WRONG - never manually insert bullet characters
   146	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("• Item")] })  // BAD
   147	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("\u2022 Item")] })  // BAD
   148	
   149	// ✅ CORRECT - use numbering config with LevelFormat.BULLET
   150	const doc = new Document({
   151	  numbering: {
   152	    config: [
   153	      { reference: "bullets",
   154	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.BULLET, text: "•", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   155	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   156	      { reference: "numbers",
   157	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.DECIMAL, text: "%1.", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   158	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   159	    ]
   160	  },
   161	  sections: [{
   162	    children: [
   163	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "bullets", level: 0 },
   164	        children: [new TextRun("Bullet item")] }),
   165	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "numbers", level: 0 },
   166	        children: [new TextRun("Numbered item")] }),
   167	    ]
   168	  }]
   169	});
   170	
   171	// ⚠️ Each reference creates INDEPENDENT numbering
   172	// Same reference = continues (1,2,3 then 4,5,6)
   173	// Different reference = restarts (1,2,3 then 1,2,3)
   174	```
   175	
   176	### Tables
   177	
   178	**CRITICAL: Tables need dual widths** - set both `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on each cell. Without both, tables render incorrectly on some platforms.
   179	
   180	```javascript
   181	// CRITICAL: Always set table width for consistent rendering
   182	// CRITICAL: Use ShadingType.CLEAR (not SOLID) to prevent black backgrounds
   183	const border = { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 1, color: "CCCCCC" };
   184	const borders = { top: border, bottom: border, left: border, right: border };
   185	
   186	new Table({
   187	  width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Always use DXA (percentages break in Google Docs)
   188	  columnWidths: [4680, 4680], // Must sum to table width (DXA: 1440 = 1 inch)
   189	  rows: [
   190	    new TableRow({
   191	      children: [
   192	        new TableCell({
   193	          borders,
   194	          width: { size: 4680, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Also set on each cell
   195	          shading: { fill: "D5E8F0", type: ShadingType.CLEAR }, // CLEAR not SOLID
   196	          margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }, // Cell padding (internal, not added to width)
   197	          children: [new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("Cell")] })]
   198	        })
   199	      ]
   200	    })
   201	  ]
   202	})
   203	```
   204	
   205	**Table width calculation:**
   206	
   207	Always use `WidthType.DXA` — `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` breaks in Google Docs.
   208	
   209	```javascript
   210	// Table width = sum of columnWidths = content width
   211	// US Letter with 1" margins: 12240 - 2880 = 9360 DXA
   212	width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA },
   213	columnWidths: [7000, 2360]  // Must sum to table width
   214	```
   215	
   216	**Width rules:**
	< truncated lines 217-374 >
   375	}]
   376	```
   377	
   378	### Critical Rules for docx-js
   379	
   380	- **Set page size explicitly** - docx-js defaults to A4; use US Letter (12240 x 15840 DXA) for US documents
   381	- **Landscape: pass portrait dimensions** - docx-js swaps width/height internally; pass short edge as `width`, long edge as `height`, and set `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE`
   382	- **Never use `\n`** - use separate Paragraph elements
   383	- **Never use unicode bullets** - use `LevelFormat.BULLET` with numbering config
   384	- **PageBreak must be in Paragraph** - standalone creates invalid XML
   385	- **ImageRun requires `type`** - always specify png/jpg/etc
   386	- **Always set table `width` with DXA** - never use `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` (breaks in Google Docs)
   387	- **Tables need dual widths** - `columnWidths` array AND cell `width`, both must match
   388	- **Table width = sum of columnWidths** - for DXA, ensure they add up exactly
   389	- **Always add cell margins** - use `margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }` for readable padding
   390	- **Use `ShadingType.CLEAR`** - never SOLID for table shading
   391	- **Never use tables as dividers/rules** - cells have minimum height and render as empty boxes (including in headers/footers); use `border: { bottom: { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 6, color: "2E75B6", space: 1 } }` on a Paragraph instead. For two-column footers, use tab stops (see Tab Stops section), not tables
   392	- **TOC requires HeadingLevel only** - no custom styles on heading paragraphs
   393	- **Override built-in styles** - use exact IDs: "Heading1", "Heading2", etc.
   394	- **Include `outlineLevel`** - required for TOC (0 for H1, 1 for H2, etc.)
   395	
   396	---
   397	
   398	## Editing Existing Documents
   399	
   400	**Follow all 3 steps in order.**
   401	
   402	### Step 1: Unpack
   403	```bash
   404	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
   405	```
   406	Extracts XML, pretty-prints, merges adjacent runs, and converts smart quotes to XML entities (`“` etc.) so they survive editing. Use `--merge-runs false` to skip run merging.
   407	
   408	### Step 2: Edit XML
   409	
   410	Edit files in `unpacked/word/`. See XML Reference below for patterns.
   411	
   412	**Use "Claude" as the author** for tracked changes and comments, unless the user explicitly requests use of a different name.
   413	
   414	**Use the Edit tool directly for string replacement. Do not write Python scripts.** Scripts introduce unnecessary complexity. The Edit tool shows exactly what is being replaced.
   415	
   416	**CRITICAL: Use smart quotes for new content.** When adding text with apostrophes or quotes, use XML entities to produce smart quotes:
   417	```xml
   418	<!-- Use these entities for professional typography -->
   419	<w:t>Here’s a quote: “Hello”</w:t>
   420	```
   421	| Entity | Character |
   422	|--------|-----------|
   423	| `‘` | ‘ (left single) |
   424	| `’` | ’ (right single / apostrophe) |
   425	| `“` | “ (left double) |
   426	| `”` | ” (right double) |
   427	
   428	**Adding comments:** Use `comment.py` to handle boilerplate across multiple XML files (text must be pre-escaped XML):
   429	```bash
   430	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Comment text with & and ’"
   431	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 1 "Reply text" --parent 0  # reply to comment 0
   432	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Text" --author "Custom Author"  # custom author name
   433	```
   434	Then add markers to document.xml (see Comments in XML Reference).
   435	
   436	### Step 3: Pack
   437	```bash
   438	python scripts/office/pack.py unpacked/ output.docx --original document.docx
   439	```
   440	Validates with auto-repair, condenses XML, and creates DOCX. Use `--validate false` to skip.
   441	
   442	**Auto-repair will fix:**
   443	- `durableId` >= 0x7FFFFFFF (regenerates valid ID)
   444	- Missing `xml:space="preserve"` on `<w:t>` with whitespace
   445	
   446	**Auto-repair won't fix:**
   447	- Malformed XML, invalid element nesting, missing relationships, schema violations
   448	
   449	### Common Pitfalls
   450	
   451	- **Replace entire `<w:r>` elements**: When adding tracked changes, replace the whole `<w:r>...</w:r>` block with `<w:del>...<w:ins>...` as siblings. Don't inject tracked change tags inside a run.
   452	- **Preserve `<w:rPr>` formatting**: Copy the original run's `<w:rPr>` block into your tracked change runs to maintain bold, font size, etc.
   453	
   454	---
   455	
   456	## XML Reference
   457	
   458	### Schema Compliance
   459	
   460	- **Element order in `<w:pPr>`**: `<w:pStyle>`, `<w:numPr>`, `<w:spacing>`, `<w:ind>`, `<w:jc>`, `<w:rPr>` last
   461	- **Whitespace**: Add `xml:space="preserve"` to `<w:t>` with leading/trailing spaces
   462	- **RSIDs**: Must be 8-digit hex (e.g., `00AB1234`)
   463	
   464	### Tracked Changes
   465	
   466	**Insertion:**
   467	```xml
   468	<w:ins w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   469	  <w:r><w:t>inserted text</w:t></w:r>
   470	</w:ins>
   471	```
   472	
   473	**Deletion:**
   474	```xml
   475	<w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   476	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   477	</w:del>
   478	```
   479	
   480	**Inside `<w:del>`**: Use `<w:delText>` instead of `<w:t>`, and `<w:delInstrText>` instead of `<w:instrText>`.
   481	
   482	**Minimal edits** - only mark what changes:
   483	```xml
   484	<!-- Change "30 days" to "60 days" -->
   485	<w:r><w:t>The term is </w:t></w:r>
   486	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   487	  <w:r><w:delText>30</w:delText></w:r>
   488	</w:del>
   489	<w:ins w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   490	  <w:r><w:t>60</w:t></w:r>
   491	</w:ins>
   492	<w:r><w:t> days.</w:t></w:r>
   493	```
   494	
   495	**Deleting entire paragraphs/list items** - when removing ALL content from a paragraph, also mark the paragraph mark as deleted so it merges with the next paragraph. Add `<w:del/>` inside `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`:
   496	```xml
   497	<w:p>
   498	  <w:pPr>
   499	    <w:numPr>...</w:numPr>  <!-- list numbering if present -->
   500	    <w:rPr>
   501	      <w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>
   502	    </w:rPr>
   503	  </w:pPr>
   504	  <w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   505	    <w:r><w:delText>Entire paragraph content being deleted...</w:delText></w:r>
   506	  </w:del>
   507	</w:p>
   508	```
   509	Without the `<w:del/>` in `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`, accepting changes leaves an empty paragraph/list item.
   510	
   511	**Rejecting another author's insertion** - nest deletion inside their insertion:
   512	```xml
   513	<w:ins w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   514	  <w:del w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   515	    <w:r><w:delText>their inserted text</w:delText></w:r>
   516	  </w:del>
   517	</w:ins>
   518	```
   519	
   520	**Restoring another author's deletion** - add insertion after (don't modify their deletion):
   521	```xml
   522	<w:del w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   523	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   524	</w:del>
   525	<w:ins w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   526	  <w:r><w:t>deleted text</w:t></w:r>
   527	</w:ins>
   528	```
   529	
   530	### Comments
   531	
   532	After running `comment.py` (see Step 2), add markers to document.xml. For replies, use `--parent` flag and nest markers inside the parent's.
   533	
   534	**CRITICAL: `<w:commentRangeStart>` and `<w:commentRangeEnd>` are siblings of `<w:r>`, never inside `<w:r>`.**
   535	
   536	```xml
   537	<!-- Comment markers are direct children of w:p, never inside w:r -->
   538	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   539	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   540	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted</w:delText></w:r>
   541	</w:del>
   542	<w:r><w:t> more text</w:t></w:r>
   543	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   544	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   545	
   546	<!-- Comment 0 with reply 1 nested inside -->
   547	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   548	  <w:commentRangeStart w:id="1"/>
   549	  <w:r><w:t>text</w:t></w:r>
   550	  <w:commentRangeEnd w:id="1"/>
   551	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   552	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   553	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="1"/></w:r>
   554	```
   555	
   556	### Images
   557	
   558	1. Add image file to `word/media/`
   559	2. Add relationship to `word/_rels/document.xml.rels`:
   560	```xml
   561	<Relationship Id="rId5" Type=".../image" Target="media/image1.png"/>
   562	```
   563	3. Add content type to `[Content_Types].xml`:
   564	```xml
   565	<Default Extension="png" ContentType="image/png"/>
   566	```
   567	4. Reference in document.xml:
   568	```xml
   569	<w:drawing>
   570	  <wp:inline>
   571	    <wp:extent cx="914400" cy="914400"/>  <!-- EMUs: 914400 = 1 inch -->
   572	    <a:graphic>
   573	      <a:graphicData uri=".../picture">
   574	        <pic:pic>
   575	          <pic:blipFill><a:blip r:embed="rId5"/></pic:blipFill>
   576	        </pic:pic>
   577	      </a:graphicData>
   578	    </a:graphic>
   579	  </wp:inline>
   580	</w:drawing>
   581	```
   582	
   583	---
   584	
   585	## Dependencies
   586	
   587	- **pandoc**: Text extraction
   588	- **docx**: `npm install -g docx` (new documents)
   589	- **LibreOffice**: PDF conversion (auto-configured for sandboxed environments via `scripts/office/soffice.py`)
   590	- **Poppler**: `pdftoppm` for images

input.file_text:
# AI Code Review Framework — Feature List

> Status: Draft v0.1 — scope definition, pre-specification
> Last updated: 2026-03-18

---

## Core

- Git diff as the universal input unit
- Judges as plug-and-play units, each defined by a `SKILL.md` file
- Each judge evaluates exactly one aspect of the code, scored 0–10
- Per-judge score + aggregate overall score
- SARIF as the standard output format (compatible with GitHub, GitLab, VS Code)

---

## Judges

- Each judge is independent and interchangeable
- A judge may internally use other skills
- Judges can be composed into named packs (e.g. "Uncle Bob pack", "Security pack")
- Community ecosystem of shareable, open-source judges

---

## CLI Interface

- Progressive disclosure — summary first, details on demand
- Queryable by judge, by issue, by file
- `--json` output flag for agent consumption
- Rich terminal output for human readability
- Per-session judge reprioritization (developer or agent can promote/demote judges)

---

## Integrations

- Git hook support (post-commit)
- CI/CD integration (GitLab CI, GitHub Actions)
- SARIF output → native PR annotations (GitHub, GitLab)

---

## Dashboard

- Live view of all judge scores for the current session
- Agent activity tracking via CLI call observation
- Score history across commits (trend per judge)

---

## General

- Fully local — no subscription, no external server required
- Vendor-agnostic — works with any LLM provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, local models, etc.)
- Open-source

---

## Out of Scope (for now)

- Skill benchmarking / skill testing pipeline
- Multi-agent skill evaluation framework
- Fine-tuning judges on project-specific examples

Good research. Let me summarize the findings clearly for the user.

Key findings:
- pre-commit (Python): still the standard for Python ecosystem, large community hook catalog
- husky (JS/TS): dominant in JS/TS world, ~5M weekly downloads, but JS-only
- lefthook (Go binary): language-agnostic, parallel execution, faster, growing (~1.1M weekly downloads), works for both Python and JS/TS projects - this is the key insight
- The answer to "write once" is lefthook - it's language-agnostic and can run any command

The key insight: lefthook is the bridge. It's a single tool that works for both Python and JS/TS ecosystems, runs any CLI command, and doesn't require Node.js or Python to be installed.Dobra wiadomość — jest rozwiązanie, które eliminuje problem "pisać dwa razy".

---

### Stan ekosystemu

**pre-commit** (Python) i **husky** (JS/TS) to wciąż industry standard w swoich niszach. Husky ma 23M pobrań tygodniowo na npm, pre-commit ~344K. Nie ma nic co by je wyparło — obie community są żywe.

Ale jest trzeci gracz który rośnie i rozwiązuje Twój problem:

**Lefthook** — napisany w Go, uruchamia hooki równolegle, ~10x szybszy od husky dla dużych projektów, nie wymaga Node.js. Językowo-agnostyczny — frontend, backend i DevOps mogą współdzielić hook logic bez context switching. ~1.1M pobrań tygodniowo i rośnie.

---

### Odpowiedź na Twoje pytanie

**Lefthook rozwiązuje problem "nie chcę pisać dwa razy".**

Twoje narzędzie jest napisane w Pythonie — to jest jeden executable, jeden CLI, `code-review run`. Lefthook po prostu go wywołuje, niezależnie od tego czy repo jest pythonowe czy TS-owe:

```yaml
# lefthook.yml — działa w KAŻDYM repo, niezależnie od języka
post-commit:
  commands:
    code-review:
      run: code-review run --staged
```

Developer w projekcie JS dodaje ten plik i gotowe — nie obchodzi go że tool jest napisany w Pythonie. Developer w projekcie Python — tak samo.

---

### Mapowanie na ekosystemy

| Ekosystem | Narzędzie | Jak wywołuje Twój tool |
|-----------|-----------|------------------------|
| Python | pre-commit | `local hook` → `code-review run` |
| JS/TS | husky | `.husky/post-commit` → `code-review run` |
| Dowolny | **lefthook** | `lefthook.yml` → `code-review run` |

---

### Rekomendacja

Napisz tool raz w Pythonie. Dostarcz **trzy gotowe snippety** w dokumentacji — jeden dla lefthook, jeden dla pre-commit, jeden dla husky. To wystarczy żeby pokryć 95% developerów, a Ty nie duplikujesz żadnego kodu.

Na PoC — zacznij od lefthook, bo to jeden config który możesz pokazać każdemu niezależnie od stosu.

content.text:
The other tools, including pre-commit (despite its name), lefthook, husky, and overcommit, are all capable of managing many types of hooks. Nonetheless, the documentation for each of these tools has large sections showing how to orchestrate code quality tools as part of your pre-commit hooks.

What’s a code quality meta tool? It’s a tool that lets you orchestrate many linting and formatting tools to operate on an entire project which may contain many languages. Examples include tidyall (which I maintain), pre-commit, lefthook, husky, overcommit, and precious (my new project in this space). It’s worth noting that only tidyall and precious describe themselves as being focused on tool orchestration. The others all describe themselves as systems for managing Git hooks. The other tools, including pre-commit (despite its name), lefthook, husky, and overcommit, are all capable of managing many types of hooks. Nonetheless, the documentation for each of these tools has large sections showing how to orchestrate code quality tools as part of your pre-commit hooks. In addition, each tool allows you to run the tools outside of git hooks so you can run them from the CLI and in CI.

It’s not clear to me, but I think many people combine lint-staged with husky, which allows you to select files in various ways. From looking at the code, I think all commands are run in parallel by default, but the docs don’t really clarify this. There are no caching options or support for incremental linting. So while it’s quite flexible it also doesn’t do much to help you. If pre-commit is the maximum hand holding option, this one is the least, with all the others in between. Alright, the last one before the last one. It’s another hook manager, this time in Ruby. You install it with the gem tool, so I’d assume it’s as annoying as JS or Perl tools if you’re not familiar with the language. Its first release was in May of 2013 and it looks to be active developed. Configuration is in YAML. Plugins are defined externally as Ruby classes, much like tidyall.

The pre-commit project itself maintains a huge number of plugin definitions, and some tools include pre-commit config in their repo directly. It’s also worth noting that you can configure which files a plugin runs on locally. The yamllint config above just says it operates on YAML files, but you can narrow that down to specific parts of your project. All of this is very cool but there is one big downside. You’re at the mercy of the person who makes this remote repo for much of the tool’s config. For one small example, the golangci-lint repo’s plugin config says to run golangci-lint run --fix. If you didn’t want the --fix flag you have to find another repo that defines a golangci-lint hook instead. Except that other one I linked always runs it as golangci-lint run --new-from-rev="$(git rev-parse HEAD)". So that’s going to make it impossible to just run this tool across your entire current codebase.

But at the same time, I wouldn’t be that excited to use it. I really dislike the way I have to go look at config in all these different repos just to find one that works the way I want, or maybe to find out that none of them work the way I want. If I were to use pre-commit, I think I’d just define all of my hooks locally. That does throw away some of the convenience of pre-commit, but I’d still be able to take advantage of its great support for managing tools and dependencies across many languages. The lefthook tool is written in Go. They’re using goreleaser to publish binary releases to GitHub, so installation is trivial. You can download a binary from the releases page or use godownloader to automate this completely. It was first released in February of 2019, and appears to be under active development. Compared to pre-commit, lefthook is much simpler.

In the world of Git hooks, two popular tools often come up: Lefthook and Husky. Both are designed to manage Git hooks efficiently, but they have different features and use cases. This article will compare the benefits of Lefthook over Husky and provide a step-by-step guide on how to use Lefthook in your projects. Performance Lefthook is known for its performance. It is written in Go, which makes it faster and more efficient compared to Husky, which is written in JavaScript. This can be particularly beneficial for large projects with many hooks. Parallel Execution Lefthook supports parallel execution of hooks out of the box. This means that multiple hooks can run simultaneously, reducing the overall time taken for pre-commit or pre-push operations. Husky, on the other hand, executes hooks sequentially. Configuration Lefthook uses a YAML configuration file, which is straightforward and easy to read.

The check-code script is what we typically use in our pre-commit hook to ensure both linting and formatting are performed before each commit. Create a lefthook.yml file in the root of your project. This file will define the hooks you want to use. Here is an example configuration: pre-commit: commands: check-code: run: npm run check-code update-index: run: git update-index --again · This is a base example that we use here at Quave. We added the check-code to run our eslint and prettier. The update-index command is crucial here. When we run ESLint with the --fix option and Prettier, they modify our files to fix linting issues and format the code. These modifications would normally be left unstaged, meaning they wouldn't be included in the current commit. By running git update-index --again, we ensure that these automatic fixes are included in the current commit.

Now, when you commit or push changes, Lefthook will automatically run the defined hooks. You can also manually run Lefthook to test your configuration: ... Lefthook offers several advantages over Husky, including better performance, parallel execution, and greater flexibility. In modern software development, maintaining code quality and consistency is important. Unlike other approaches, using git hooks for this matter has the advantage of providing immediate feedback. The pre-commit and lefthook projects are two popular options for managing git hooks. In this article, I’ll compare their features, ease of use, community support, and performance to help you decide which tool is best suited for your project. Pre-commit is a versatile git hooks manager written in Python and was created in 2014. Its primary goal is to catch and address issues such as missing semicolons, trailing whitespace, and debug statements before code review, allowing reviewers to focus on the architecture and logic of changes. The installation and configuration are designed to be user-friendly, enabling teams to quickly set up and enforce coding standards.

Written in Go, lefthook is a powerful git hooks manager that debuted in 2019. Given their shared goals, lefthook and pre-commit share many features. Lefthook also offers straightforward installation, configuration and ease of use. While lefthook has a beta remotes feature, which enables the use of remote hooks, this capability is currently limited to flat reuse and lacks advanced options for configuring remote hooks. On this point, lefthook is behind pre-commit, which offers configurable remote hooks and a large catalog of community hooks. On the other hand, lefthook has a significant advantage in performance, especially with its support for concurrent execution. Like pre-commit, hooks run sequentially by default, but you can enable parallel execution using the parallel parameter. Let’s adapt the configuration we previously created to lefthook’s format and observe the differences.

I was curious to see if it was possible to use both simultaneously. I wouldn’t necessarily recommend it, but it can be done with a small trick! If you’re interested, I’ve explained how to do that in the dotdc/test-lefthook-and-pre-commit repository.

Choosing the right Git hooks manager directly impacts code quality, developer experience, and CI/CD performance. Lefthook and Husky are two widely used tools that automate Git hook workflows like pre-commit, pre-push, and commit-msg. Both tools aim to enforce consistent code standards, prevent broken commits, and integrate seamlessly into the development process. However, their design, performance, and ecosystem compatibility differ significantly. Lefthook supports YAML configuration and doesn’t depend on any specific runtime like Node.js or Ruby. It’s suitable for teams working across multiple languages—frontend, backend, and DevOps engineers can share hook logic without context switching. Husky is a popular Git hooks manager built for the JavaScript ecosystem. It integrates directly with Node.js and NPM-based projects and is often used alongside tools like lint-staged, ESLint, Prettier, and commitlint. Originally, Husky used the package.json file for configuration. Since version 5, it shifted to using a .husky/ folder with shell scripts for each Git hook. This change gave users more control but also increased the manual setup burden. Husky excels in simple JavaScript or TypeScript projects where developers want a quick and standard setup. It’s widely adopted and maintained, with over 7 million weekly downloads on NPM, making it a default choice for many frontend teams.

One major technical difference lies in execution. Lefthook executes hooks through its binary, which is faster and allows for caching. Husky runs each hook sequentially using bash, which may slow down pre-commit checks in large projects. Lefthook fits well in environments where performance and cross-language support matter. Monorepos with frontend, backend, and infra code benefit from a single Git hook manager that doesn’t rely on a Node.js runtime. CI environments also favor Lefthook. Since it ships as a binary, it can run in Docker images or lightweight CI containers without needing to install Node modules. This reduces setup time and avoids bloated build steps. Teams that need to filter hooks by file path or extension also benefit. Lefthook allows specifying file patterns directly in its configuration, so hooks only run when relevant files change—critical for large teams trying to speed up feedback loops.

What’s a code quality meta tool? It’s a tool that lets you orchestrate many linting and formatting tools to operate on an entire project which may contain many languages. Examples include tidyall (which I maintain), pre-commit, lefthook, husky, overcommit, and precious (my new project in this space). It’s worth noting that only tidyall and precious describe themselves as being focused on tool orchestration. The others all describe themselves as systems for managing Git hooks. The other tools, including pre-commit (despite its name), lefthook, husky, and overcommit, are all capable of managing many types of hooks. Nonetheless, the documentation for each of these tools has large sections showing how to orchestrate code quality tools as part of your pre-commit hooks. In addition, each tool allows you to run the tools outside of git hooks so you can run them from the CLI and in CI.

Overall, lefthook is fairly minimal compared to other tools. Because it’s all config based, and you can put shell commands in the config directly, it’s quite flexible. From what I can see, it doesn’t have any caching built in, nor does it support incremental linting. The husky tool is dog themed, which is a clear point in its favor, as opposed to focusing on cleaning (no fun), violence (fun?), or actually naming itself after exactly what it’s for, like a boring boomer or something. Installation is via npm or yarn, which is about as annoying as using the CPAN tools in my experience. It looks like a fairly JavaScript focused tool. It’s configured through entries in a project’s package.json file. If your project is in JS this is very convenient. If it’s not it will feel weird, but it’s just yet another config file in your project root.

Either way, I applaud it for not using YAML like pre-commit and lefthook. While my current favorite config language is TOML, I’ll take pretty much anything over YAML except XML. Running tools from husky is done by specifying shell commands in its config or by writing a config file in JS which defines the commands to be run. It really doesn’t have much in the way of other features. For example, there is no way to specify files to run against in your config. It’s not clear to me, but I think many people combine lint-staged with husky, which allows you to select files in various ways. From looking at the code, I think all commands are run in parallel by default, but the docs don’t really clarify this. There are no caching options or support for incremental linting. So while it’s quite flexible it also doesn’t do much to help you. If pre-commit is the maximum hand holding option, this one is the least, with all the others in between.

But at the same time, I wouldn’t be that excited to use it. I really dislike the way I have to go look at config in all these different repos just to find one that works the way I want, or maybe to find out that none of them work the way I want. If I were to use pre-commit, I think I’d just define all of my hooks locally. That does throw away some of the convenience of pre-commit, but I’d still be able to take advantage of its great support for managing tools and dependencies across many languages. The lefthook tool is written in Go. They’re using goreleaser to publish binary releases to GitHub, so installation is trivial. You can download a binary from the releases page or use godownloader to automate this completely. It was first released in February of 2019, and appears to be under active development. Compared to pre-commit, lefthook is much simpler.

Once configured, run lefthook install to set up the hooks. ... Husky is a widely-used hook manager in the JavaScript ecosystem. Husky doesn’t hide unstaged changes and is not able to provide the list of staged files. This is why it is often used in tandem with another tool such as lint-staged or git-format-staged. If your project contains a package.json, you can automatically set up husky hooks upon package installation using scripts.prepare: ... The configuration of lint-staged is directly embedded in package.json. Here’s some example of commands that you could find useful when running the Git hooks: ... "biome check --write --organize-imports-enabled=false --no-errors-on-unmatched", // format and apply safe fixes ... "biome check --write --unsafe --no-errors-on-unmatched", // Format, sort imports, lints, apply safe/unsafe fixes ... Remember to use the CLI option --no-errors-on-unmatched in your command, to silent possible errors in case no files are processed.

Lefthook provides a fast, cross-platform, and dependency-free hook manager. It can be installed via NPM. Add a file named lefthook.yml at the root of your Git repository. Some examples of Lefthook configurations: ... run: npx @biomejs/biome check --no-errors-on-unmatched --files-ignore-unknown=true --colors=off {staged_files} Format, lint, and apply safe code fixes before committing ... run: npx @biomejs/biome check --write --no-errors-on-unmatched --files-ignore-unknown=true --colors=off {staged_files} ... run: npx @biomejs/biome check --no-errors-on-unmatched --files-ignore-unknown=true --colors=off {push_files} Note that you don’t need to use both glob and --files-ignore-unknown=true. Using only --files-ignore-unknown=true allows handling files supported in the present and in the future by Biome. If you wish more control over which files are handled, you should use glob.

content.text:
Dobra wiadomość — jest rozwiązanie, które eliminuje problem "pisać dwa razy".

---

### Stan ekosystemu

**pre-commit** (Python) i **husky** (JS/TS) to wciąż industry standard w swoich niszach. Husky ma 23M pobrań tygodniowo na npm, pre-commit ~344K. Nie ma nic co by je wyparło — obie community są żywe.

Ale jest trzeci gracz który rośnie i rozwiązuje Twój problem:

**Lefthook** — napisany w Go, uruchamia hooki równolegle, ~10x szybszy od husky dla dużych projektów, nie wymaga Node.js. Językowo-agnostyczny — frontend, backend i DevOps mogą współdzielić hook logic bez context switching. ~1.1M pobrań tygodniowo i rośnie.

---

### Odpowiedź na Twoje pytanie

**Lefthook rozwiązuje problem "nie chcę pisać dwa razy".**

Twoje narzędzie jest napisane w Pythonie — to jest jeden executable, jeden CLI, `code-review run`. Lefthook po prostu go wywołuje, niezależnie od tego czy repo jest pythonowe czy TS-owe:

```yaml
# lefthook.yml — działa w KAŻDYM repo, niezależnie od języka
post-commit:
  commands:
    code-review:
      run: code-review run --staged
```

Developer w projekcie JS dodaje ten plik i gotowe — nie obchodzi go że tool jest napisany w Pythonie. Developer w projekcie Python — tak samo.

---

### Mapowanie na ekosystemy

| Ekosystem | Narzędzie | Jak wywołuje Twój tool |
|-----------|-----------|------------------------|
| Python | pre-commit | `local hook` → `code-review run` |
| JS/TS | husky | `.husky/post-commit` → `code-review run` |
| Dowolny | **lefthook** | `lefthook.yml` → `code-review run` |

---

### Rekomendacja

Napisz tool raz w Pythonie. Dostarcz **trzy gotowe snippety** w dokumentacji — jeden dla lefthook, jeden dla pre-commit, jeden dla husky. To wystarczy żeby pokryć 95% developerów, a Ty nie duplikujesz żadnego kodu.

Na PoC — zacznij od lefthook, bo to jeden config który możesz pokazać każdemu niezależnie od stosu.

The user is making an excellent point about tool fitness for purpose. DeepEval is a testing framework — it's designed to be run as tests (via pytest), not as a production CLI tool. Using it as the backbone of a standalone CLI tool would be like using Cypress for scraping — technically possible but wrong tool for the job.

They want to understand the architecture: should they use DeepEval or build directly on top of the Anthropic SDK/LiteLLM?Bardzo trafna analogia. Masz rację.

DeepEval jest frameworkiem testowym — jego "unit" to `pytest test case`, jego output to test report, jego CI/CD integracja zakłada że jesteś w pipeline testowym. Używanie go jako silnika standalone CLI tool to jak używanie pytest jako biblioteki do obsługi HTTP requestów — da się, ale walczysz z narzędziem zamiast z problemem.

---

### Co naprawdę potrzebujesz

Twój tool potrzebuje tylko jednej rzeczy z całego ekosystemu evals: **wywołać LLM z promptem sędziego i sparsować odpowiedź**. To jest dosłownie kilkanaście linii kodu.

```python
# to jest cały "framework" którego potrzebujesz
import anthropic, json

def run_judge(skill_md: str, diff: str) -> dict:
    client = anthropic.Anthropic()
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        system=skill_md,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": diff}]
    )
    return json.loads(response.content[0].text)
```

DeepEval siedzi nad tym i dodaje: pytest integration, test reports, dataset management, metric objects. Nic z tego nie potrzebujesz w standalone CLI tool.

### Stack dla Twojego projektu

```
anthropic SDK (lub litellm jeśli chcesz vendor-agnostic)
    ↓ wywołuje LLM
rich
    ↓ terminal output
click lub typer
    ↓ CLI interface
sarif-tools lub ręczny JSON
    ↓ SARIF output
watchdog
    ↓ dashboard file watching
```

Żadnych frameworków testowych. Proste, małe zależności, działa jako normalny CLI tool.

### Gdzie DeepEval ma sens w tym projekcie

Tylko w jednym miejscu — jeśli będziesz **testował samych sędziów** (ten wątek o skill benchmarkingu który odłożyliśmy na później). Wtedy tak, DeepEval jest właściwym narzędziem. Ale to jest osobna warstwa, nie core tool.

Dobry instynkt. Pozwól że najpierw nazwę co zyskujesz, a potem szczerze o słabych stronach.

---

### Co zyskujesz

Niektóre zasady są **lokalne** — naming, magic numbers, no-comments. Diff to wszystko czego potrzebują. One-shot wystarczy.

Inne zasady są **systemowe** z natury — SRP, dependency inversion, architektura warstw. Żeby ocenić SRP w jednym pliku, sędzia musi wiedzieć czy ta odpowiedzialność już istnieje gdzieś indziej w systemie. Bez kontekstu repo odpowie na pytanie "czy ta klasa ma jedną odpowiedzialność?" zamiast na "czy ten system ma właściwy podział odpowiedzialności".

Tryb agentowy daje mu narzędzia: przeczytaj ten plik, znajdź wszystkie klasy które dziedziczą po tej bazie, sprawdź jak to jest zrobione w podobnych modułach. To jest jakościowo inny poziom oceny.

---

### Słabe strony

**Koszt i czas.** One-shot sędzia to jeden API call, sekunda, grosze. Agent-sędzia to N callów, potencjalnie dziesiątki sekund, wielokrotnie droższy. Przy post-commit hooku który odpala 8 sędziów, 3 z nich agentowych — możesz czekać minutę i zapłacić $0.10 za każdy commit. To szybko boli.

**Niedeterminizm rośnie.** One-shot sędzia wywołany dwa razy na tym samym diffie da podobny wynik. Agent może pójść inną ścieżką eksploracji i dostać inny wynik — bo trafił na inny plik najpierw, bo zrobił inne tool calls. Porównywanie wersji skilla staje się trudniejsze.

**Trudniejsze testowanie sędziów.** Jak benchmarkujesz agent-sędziego? Musisz mieć całe repo jako fixture, nie tylko diff. Infra testowa jest znacznie cięższa.

**Ryzyko rabbit hole.** Agent który może czytać dowolne pliki może pójść za daleko — przeczytać pół repo żeby ocenić jeden diff. Potrzebujesz budżetu na tool calls albo depth limit.

---

### Czy rozbijać na dwa typy, czy jeden z dwoma trybami?

Jeden judge, dwa tryby — to mi się bardziej podoba architektonicznie. Powód: sędzia definiuje **co oceniać**, nie **jak głęboko szukać**. Tryb to parametr wywołania, nie właściwość sędziego.

```yaml
# w SKILL.md sędziego
mode: agent          # one-shot | agent | auto
tools:               # tylko dla trybu agent
  - read_file
  - search_symbol
  - grep
max_tool_calls: 10   # hard limit
```

Tryb `auto` byłby najciekawszy — sędzia sam decyduje czy diff wystarczy, czy musi sięgnąć głębiej. Ale to złożoność na później.

---

### Praktyczna granica dla PoC

Na PoC zrobiłbym tylko one-shot, ale z interfejsem który już uwzględnia przyszły agent mode. Tzn. `run_judge(diff, mode="one-shot", repo_context=None)` — sygnatura gotowa na rozszerzenie, implementacja agentowa na później.

# AI Code Review Framework — Feature List

> Version: 2.0
> Last updated: 2026-03-18
> Changelog: Added judge modes, JUDGE.md spec, agent capabilities, traces, budget controls, hook integrations, LLM abstraction

---

## Core

- Git diff as the universal input unit
- Judges as plug-and-play units, each defined by a `JUDGE.md` file
- `JUDGE.md` uses YAML frontmatter (same convention as `SKILL.md`)
- Each judge evaluates exactly one aspect of the code, scored 0–10
- Per-judge score + aggregate overall score
- SARIF as the standard output format (compatible with GitHub, GitLab, VS Code)

---

## Judge Definition (JUDGE.md)

- YAML frontmatter: `name`, `version`, `mode`, `tools`, `max_tool_calls`, `timeout_seconds`
- Body: the judge's system prompt
- Three execution modes per judge:
  - `one-shot` — single LLM call, diff only
  - `agent` — multi-step, can explore repo via tools
  - `auto` — judge decides whether diff is sufficient or deeper exploration is needed
- Agent-mode tools (configurable per judge): `read_file`, `search_symbol`, `grep`, and others
- Hard limits: `max_tool_calls` and `timeout_seconds` per judge invocation

---

## Judge Types

- **One-shot judges** — operate purely on the diff (e.g. naming, magic numbers, no-comments)
- **Agent judges** — use diff as entry point, explore repo for big-picture context (e.g. SRP, architecture, dependency structure)
- Agent judges can suggest changes outside the files in the diff
- Agent judges leave execution traces (files visited, patterns found) for observability

---

## Judges Ecosystem

- Each judge is independent and interchangeable
- A judge may internally use other skills
- Judges can be composed into named packs (e.g. "Uncle Bob pack", "Security pack")
- Community ecosystem of shareable, open-source judges
- Community quality signal via stars/usage, not mandatory benchmarking

---

## CLI Interface

- Standalone usage — single command, no setup required
- Progressive disclosure — summary first, details on demand
- Queryable by judge, by issue, by file
- `--json` output flag for agent consumption
- Rich terminal output for human readability
- Per-session judge reprioritization (developer or agent can promote/demote judges)

---

## Git Hook Integrations

- **pre-commit** (Python ecosystem) — via local hook definition
- **husky** (JS/TS ecosystem) — via `.husky/` shell script
- One-command setup snippets provided for each
- Tool itself has no opinion on hook runner — it's just a CLI

---

## CI/CD

- GitLab CI integration
- GitHub Actions integration
- SARIF output → native PR annotations (GitHub, GitLab)

---

## Dashboard

- Live view of all judge scores for the current session
- Agent activity tracking via CLI call observation
- Score history across commits (trend per judge)

---

## Budget Controls

- Per-judge `max_tool_calls` limit (agent mode)
- Per-judge `timeout_seconds` limit
- Future: global cost budget per run

---

## LLM Backend

- PoC: Anthropic SDK (Claude)
- Future: vendor-agnostic via LiteLLM (OpenAI, Anthropic, local models, etc.)

---

## General

- Fully local — no subscription, no external server required
- Open-source

---

## Out of Scope (for now)

- Skill benchmarking / skill testing pipeline
- Multi-agent skill evaluation framework
- Fine-tuning judges on project-specific examples
- Cost budget controls (beyond time/call limits)
- `auto` mode implementation (post-PoC)
- Trace persistence across sessions

description: Create a PRD through user interview, codebase exploration, and module design, then submit as a GitHub issue. Use when user wants to write a PRD, create a product requirements document, or plan a new feature.

This skill will be invoked when the user wants to create a PRD. You may skip steps if you don't consider them necessary.

1. Ask the user for a long, detailed description of the problem they want to solve and any potential ideas for solutions.

2. Explore the repo to verify their assertions and understand the current state of the codebase.

4. Sketch out the major modules you will need to build or modify to complete the implementation. Actively look for opportunities to extract deep modules that can be tested in isolation.

Check with the user that these modules match their expectations. Check with the user which modules they want tests written for.

5. Once you have a complete understanding of the problem and solution, use the template below to write the PRD. The PRD should be submitted as a GitHub issue.

The problem that the user is facing, from the user's perspective.

The solution to the problem, from the user's perspective.

- The modules that will be built/modified
- The interfaces of those modules that will be modified

- Architectural decisions
- Schema changes

A list of testing decisions that were made. Include:

- Which modules will be tested

A description of the things that are out of scope for this PRD.

Any further notes about the feature.

description: Break a PRD into independently-grabbable GitHub issues using tracer-bullet vertical slices. Use when user wants to convert a PRD to issues, create implementation tickets, or break down a PRD into work items.

# PRD to Issues

Break a PRD into independently-grabbable GitHub issues using vertical slices (tracer bullets).

## Process

### 1. Locate the PRD

Ask the user for the PRD GitHub issue number (or URL).

If the PRD is not already in your context window, fetch it with `gh issue view <number>` (with comments).

### 2. Explore the codebase (optional)

If you have not already explored the codebase, do so to understand the current state of the code.

### 3. Draft vertical slices

Break the PRD into **tracer bullet** issues. Each issue is a thin vertical slice that cuts through ALL integration layers end-to-end, NOT a horizontal slice of one layer.

Slices may be 'HITL' or 'AFK'. HITL slices require human interaction, such as an architectural decision or a design review. AFK slices can be implemented and merged without human interaction. Prefer AFK over HITL where possible.

<vertical-slice-rules>
- Each slice delivers a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests)
- A completed slice is demoable or verifiable on its own
- Prefer many thin slices over few thick ones
</vertical-slice-rules>

### 4. Quiz the user

Present the proposed breakdown as a numbered list. For each slice, show:

- **Title**: short descriptive name
- **Type**: HITL / AFK
- **Blocked by**: which other slices (if any) must complete first
- **User stories covered**: which user stories from the PRD this addresses

Ask the user:

- Does the granularity feel right? (too coarse / too fine)
- Are the dependency relationships correct?
- Should any slices be merged or split further?
- Are the correct slices marked as HITL and AFK?

Iterate until the user approves the breakdown.

### 5. Create the GitHub issues

For each approved slice, create a GitHub issue using `gh issue create`. Use the issue body template below.

Create issues in dependency order (blockers first) so you can reference real issue numbers in the "Blocked by" field.

<issue-template>
## Parent PRD

#<prd-issue-number>

## What to build

A concise description of this vertical slice. Describe the end-to-end behavior, not layer-by-layer implementation. Reference specific sections of the parent PRD rather than duplicating content.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Criterion 1
- [ ] Criterion 2
- [ ] Criterion 3

## Blocked by

- Blocked by #<issue-number> (if any)

Or "None - can start immediately" if no blockers.

## User stories addressed

Reference by number from the parent PRD:

- User story 3
- User story 7

</issue-template>

Do NOT close or modify the parent PRD issue.

# Feature PRD Prompt

## Goal

Act as an expert Product Manager for a large-scale SaaS platform. Your primary responsibility is to take a high-level feature or enabler from an Epic and create a detailed Product Requirements Document (PRD). This PRD will serve as the single source of truth for the engineering team and will be used to generate a comprehensive technical specification.

Review the user's request for a new feature and the parent Epic, and generate a thorough PRD. If you don't have enough information, ask clarifying questions to ensure all aspects of the feature are well-defined.

## Output Format

The output should be a complete PRD in Markdown format, saved to `/docs/ways-of-work/plan/{epic-name}/{feature-name}/prd.md`.

### PRD Structure

#### 1. Feature Name

- A clear, concise, and descriptive name for the feature.

#### 2. Epic

- Link to the parent Epic PRD and Architecture documents.

#### 3. Goal

- **Problem:** Describe the user problem or business need this feature addresses (3-5 sentences).
- **Solution:** Explain how this feature solves the problem.
- **Impact:** What are the expected outcomes or metrics to be improved (e.g., user engagement, conversion rate, etc.)?

#### 4. User Personas

- Describe the target user(s) for this feature.

#### 5. User Stories

- Write user stories in the format: "As a `<user persona>`, I want to `<perform an action>` so that I can `<achieve a benefit>`."
- Cover the primary paths and edge cases.

#### 6. Requirements

- **Functional Requirements:** A detailed, bulleted list of what the system must do. Be specific and unambiguous.
- **Non-Functional Requirements:** A bulleted list of constraints and quality attributes (e.g., performance, security, accessibility, data privacy).

#### 7. Acceptance Criteria

- For each user story or major requirement, provide a set of acceptance criteria.
- Use a clear format, such as a checklist or Given/When/Then. This will be used to validate that the feature is complete and correct.

#### 8. Out of Scope

- Clearly list what is _not_ included in this feature to avoid scope creep.

## Context Template

- **Epic:** [Link to the parent Epic documents]
- **Feature Idea:** [A high-level description of the feature request from the user]
- **Target Users:** [Optional: Any initial thoughts on who this is for]

# Product Requirements Document (PRD)

## Overview

Design comprehensive, production-grade Product Requirements Documents (PRDs) that bridge the gap between business vision and technical execution. This skill works for modern software systems, ensuring that requirements are clearly defined.

## When to Use

Use this skill when:

- Starting a new product or feature development cycle
- Translating a vague idea into a concrete technical specification
- Defining requirements for AI-powered features
- Stakeholders need a unified "source of truth" for project scope
- User asks to "write a PRD", "document requirements", or "plan a feature"

---

## Operational Workflow

### Phase 1: Discovery (The Interview)

Before writing a single line of the PRD, you **MUST** interrogate the user to fill knowledge gaps. Do not assume context.

**Ask about:**

- **The Core Problem**: Why are we building this now?
- **Success Metrics**: How do we know it worked?
- **Constraints**: Budget, tech stack, or deadline?

### Phase 2: Analysis & Scoping

Synthesize the user's input. Identify dependencies and hidden complexities.

- Map out the **User Flow**.
- Define **Non-Goals** to protect the timeline.

### Phase 3: Technical Drafting

Generate the document using the **Strict PRD Schema** below.

---

## PRD Quality Standards

### Requirements Quality

Use concrete, measurable criteria. Avoid "fast", "easy", or "intuitive".

```diff
# Vague (BAD)
- The search should be fast and return relevant results.
- The UI must look modern and be easy to use.

# Concrete (GOOD)
+ The search must return results within 200ms for a 10k record dataset.
+ The search algorithm must achieve >= 85% Precision@10 in benchmark evals.
+ The UI must follow the 'Vercel/Next.js' design system and achieve 100% Lighthouse Accessibility score.
```

---

## Strict PRD Schema

You **MUST** follow this exact structure for the output:

### 1. Executive Summary

- **Problem Statement**: 1-2 sentences on the pain point.
- **Proposed Solution**: 1-2 sentences on the fix.
- **Success Criteria**: 3-5 measurable KPIs.

### 2. User Experience & Functionality

- **User Personas**: Who is this for?
- **User Stories**: `As a [user], I want to [action] so that [benefit].`
- **Acceptance Criteria**: Bulleted list of "Done" definitions for each story.
- **Non-Goals**: What are we NOT building?

### 3. AI System Requirements (If Applicable)

- **Tool Requirements**: What tools and APIs are needed?
- **Evaluation Strategy**: How to measure output quality and accuracy.

### 4. Technical Specifications

- **Architecture Overview**: Data flow and component interaction.
- **Integration Points**: APIs, DBs, and Auth.
- **Security & Privacy**: Data handling and compliance.

### 5. Risks & Roadmap

- **Phased Rollout**: MVP -> v1.1 -> v2.0.
- **Technical Risks**: Latency, cost, or dependency failures.

---

## Implementation Guidelines

### DO (Always)

- **Define Testing**: For AI systems, specify how to test and validate output quality.
- **Iterate**: Present a draft and ask for feedback on specific sections.

### DON'T (Avoid)

- **Skip Discovery**: Never write a PRD without asking at least 2 clarifying questions first.
- **Hallucinate Constraints**: If the user didn't specify a tech stack, ask or label it as `TBD`.

---

## Example: Intelligent Search System

### 1. Executive Summary

**Problem**: Users struggle to find specific documentation snippets in massive repositories.
**Solution**: An intelligent search system that provides direct answers with source citations.
**Success**:

- Reduce search time by 50%.
- Citation accuracy >= 95%.

### 2. User Stories

- **Story**: As a developer, I want to ask natural language questions so I don't have to guess keywords.
- **AC**:
  - Supports multi-turn clarification.
  - Returns code blocks with "Copy" button.

### 3. AI System Architecture

- **Tools Required**: `codesearch`, `grep`, `webfetch`.

### 4. Evaluation

- **Benchmark**: Test with 50 common developer questions.
- **Pass Rate**: 90% must match expected citations.

# CLAUDE.md — Project Context

This file gives Claude Code full context to start implementing without re-explaining decisions.

---

## What are we building

**`code-review`** — a CLI tool that runs a panel of LLM-powered judges on a git diff and produces per-principle scores (0–10) with actionable feedback.

Designed for two consumers simultaneously:
- **Developer** — Rich terminal output, progressive disclosure
- **AI agent** (Claude Code, etc.) — `--json` flag, SARIF output, queryable CLI

The key differentiator: judges are **plug-and-play JUDGE.md files**, not hardcoded rules. Anyone can write and share a judge.

---

## Key design decisions (do not revisit without reason)

| Decision | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Language | Python | Primary target community, solo dev |
| LLM backend | Anthropic SDK (PoC) | LiteLLM later for vendor-agnostic |
| CLI framework | Typer | Modern, typed, auto-docs |
| Terminal output | Rich | Industry standard for Python CLIs |
| Output format | SARIF 2.1.0 | Native GitHub/GitLab PR annotations |
| Judge definition | JUDGE.md with YAML frontmatter | Same convention as SKILL.md in this repo |
| Hook strategy | Snippets for pre-commit + husky | Tool is hook-runner agnostic |
| Commit hook type | post-commit | Feedback only, never blocks commit |
| Judge execution | one-shot for MVP, agent mode later | Validates architecture first |

---

## JUDGE.md format

```markdown
---
name: judge-naming
version: 1.0.0
mode: one-shot        # one-shot | agent (agent = post-MVP)
timeout_seconds: 30
---

You are a judge evaluating a git diff for Meaningful Names (Uncle Bob, Clean Code ch.2).

Score 0–10:
- 0: new names are misleading or cryptic
- 5: neutral, no improvement or regression
- 10: all new names clearly express intent

Respond ONLY in JSON:
{
  "score": <int 0-10>,
  "reasoning": "<1-2 sentences>",
  "violations": ["<symbol> (line N) → suggest <better-name>"],
  "improvements": ["<what was done well>"]
}
```

Judges live in `judges/` directory. The framework loads all subdirs with a `JUDGE.md`.

---

## CLI interface

```bash
# Run all loaded judges on last commit diff
code-review run

# Run on staged files (for pre-commit integration)
code-review run --staged

# Machine-readable output
code-review run --json

# Progressive disclosure
code-review show naming           # list issues for this judge
code-review show naming --issue 1 # full detail for one issue

# Reprioritize a judge for this session
code-review priority naming high
```

---

## Output formats

**Terminal (Rich):** summary table → per-judge bar + score → failing judges show top issue inline

**JSON (`--json`):** structured object, all judges, all issues, parseable by agent

**SARIF (`.code-review-report.sarif`):** written after every run, maps to file+line, compatible with GitHub/GitLab

**State file (`.code-review-state.json`):** written after every CLI call, used by dashboard to track agent activity

---

## Project structure

```
code-review/
├── CLAUDE.md                  ← this file
├── PRD.md
├── TASKS.md
├── pyproject.toml
├── code_review/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── cli.py                 ← Typer app, entry point
│   ├── runner.py              ← loads judges, runs them, collects results
│   ├── judge.py               ← Judge dataclass + JUDGE.md parser
│   ├── llm.py                 ← Anthropic SDK wrapper (thin)
│   ├── output/
│   │   ├── rich_output.py     ← terminal rendering
│   │   ├── json_output.py     ← --json serialization
│   │   └── sarif.py           ← SARIF 2.1.0 builder
│   └── state.py               ← .code-review-state.json read/write
├── judges/
│   ├── naming/JUDGE.md
│   ├── magic-numbers/JUDGE.md
│   ├── small-functions/JUDGE.md
│   ├── no-comments/JUDGE.md
│   └── srp/JUDGE.md
└── tests/
    └── ...
```

---

## Bundled judges (MVP)

All one-shot, Uncle Bob / Clean Code focused:

1. `naming` — Meaningful Names (ch.2)
2. `magic-numbers` — No Magic Numbers (ch.17)
3. `small-functions` — Small Functions (ch.3)
4. `no-comments` — No Comments / Self-Documenting Code (ch.4)
5. `srp` — Single Responsibility Principle (ch.10)

---

## Integration snippets to provide in docs

**pre-commit** (Python projects):
```yaml
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: code-review
        name: AI Code Review
        entry: code-review run --staged
        language: python
        pass_filenames: false
        stages: [post-commit]
        verbose: true
```

**husky** (JS/TS projects):
```bash
# .husky/post-commit
code-review run
```

---

## What is NOT in scope for MVP

- Agent mode for judges (repo exploration)
- Dashboard / file watcher
- CI/CD integration
- Judge packs / namespacing
- LiteLLM / vendor-agnostic backend
- Score history / trend tracking
- `auto` mode
- Community ecosystem

# PRD — AI Code Review Framework

> Version: 1.0 | Solo project | 2026-03-18

---

## Problem Statement

Developers and AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) lack fast, local, structured feedback on code quality during the commit loop. Existing tools are either too generic (one big LLM reviewer), require subscriptions, or are not designed for agent consumption. There is no open ecosystem of composable, single-purpose code quality judges that work the same way for a human at the terminal and an AI agent iterating autonomously.

---

## Solution

A CLI tool (`code-review`) that runs a configurable panel of LLM-powered judges on a git diff. Each judge is a `JUDGE.md` file — a prompt + config — that evaluates one specific principle and returns a 0–10 score with line-level feedback. Output is designed for both humans (Rich terminal) and agents (JSON + SARIF).

---

## User Stories

### Developer (human)

1. As a developer, I want to run `code-review run` after a commit and see a scored summary of code quality issues, so I can decide what to fix before pushing.
2. As a developer, I want to see only a summary by default and drill into details on demand, so my terminal isn't flooded with feedback I didn't ask for.
3. As a developer, I want to add `code-review` to my existing pre-commit or husky setup with a one-liner, so I don't have to change my workflow.
4. As a developer, I want to drop a `JUDGE.md` file into the `judges/` folder and have it picked up automatically, so I can add custom rules without touching Python code.
5. As a developer, I want SARIF output so my CI pipeline can show inline annotations on pull requests without extra integration work.

### AI agent (Claude Code, etc.)

6. As an AI agent, I want `code-review run --json` to return structured data about every judge's findings, so I can decide what to fix next without parsing human-readable text.
7. As an AI agent, I want `code-review show <judge>` to give me the list of issues for a specific principle, so I can focus on one thing at a time.
8. As an AI agent, I want `code-review show <judge> --issue <n>` to give me full context on one specific issue (file, line, reasoning, suggestion), so I can fix it precisely.
9. As an AI agent, I want to re-run a specific judge after making changes, to verify my fix improved the score before committing.

### Judge author (community)

10. As a judge author, I want to define a judge entirely in a `JUDGE.md` file using YAML frontmatter + a prompt, so I can share it without writing any Python.
11. As a judge author, I want to specify `mode: one-shot` or `mode: agent` in the frontmatter, so the framework knows how to run my judge.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### `code-review run`
- [ ] Reads git diff of last commit (or `--staged` for staged files)
- [ ] Loads all judges from `judges/` directory
- [ ] Runs each judge in parallel
- [ ] Prints Rich summary table: judge name, score bar, pass/fail icon
- [ ] Failing judges (score < threshold) show one-line top issue inline
- [ ] Writes `.code-review-report.sarif` to project root
- [ ] Writes `.code-review-state.json` to project root
- [ ] `--json` flag outputs structured JSON to stdout instead of Rich

### `code-review show <judge>`
- [ ] Lists all issues from last run for the given judge
- [ ] Each issue shows: file, line, symbol, suggestion
- [ ] Updates `.code-review-state.json` with `focus: <judge>`

### `code-review show <judge> --issue <n>`
- [ ] Shows full detail: file, line, symbol, reasoning, suggestion, code context
- [ ] Updates `.code-review-state.json` with `focus: <judge>, issue: <n>`

### JUDGE.md loading
- [ ] Parses YAML frontmatter: `name`, `version`, `mode`, `timeout_seconds`
- [ ] Uses remaining body as system prompt
- [ ] Fails gracefully if JUDGE.md is malformed (skips judge, logs warning)

### Bundled judges
- [ ] 5 judges ship with the tool: naming, magic-numbers, small-functions, no-comments, srp
- [ ] Each returns valid JSON with `score`, `reasoning`, `violations`, `improvements`

---

## Implementation Decisions

### Architecture
- Single Python package, installable via `pip install code-review` (or local `pip install -e .`)
- Typer for CLI — gives auto-generated `--help`, typed arguments, subcommands
- Judges run concurrently via `asyncio.gather()` — all judges in parallel, not sequential
- Anthropic SDK called directly — thin wrapper in `llm.py`, easy to swap later for LiteLLM
- `temperature=0` for all judge calls — determinism matters for comparing runs

### JUDGE.md
- YAML frontmatter between `---` delimiters, same convention as SKILL.md
- Body after second `---` is the raw system prompt — no processing, passed directly to LLM
- `mode` field: `one-shot` only in MVP. `agent` field parsed but not executed (logs warning)

### SARIF
- Write on every `run`, overwrite previous
- One `run` per tool invocation, one `result` per violation
- `ruleId` format: `<judge-name>/<violation-type>` e.g. `naming/non-descriptive-variable`
- `properties` includes `score` and `judge_version` for traceability

### State file
- `.code-review-state.json` — written after every CLI invocation
- Tracks: last commit, last run scores, current focus judge, last activity timestamp
- Used by future dashboard; ignored if not present

### Error handling
- LLM returns non-JSON → log warning, skip judge, do not crash run
- LLM timeout → skip judge, show `⏱ timed out` in summary
- No diff (empty commit) → print message, exit 0

---

## Out of Scope

- Agent mode execution (JUDGE.md `mode: agent` is parsed, not implemented)
- Dashboard / file watcher
- CI/CD integration (SARIF file is produced; wiring it into GitHub Actions is user's responsibility)
- Judge packs / namespacing
- LiteLLM / multi-provider support
- Score history and trend charts
- `auto` mode
- Community hub / package registry

---

## Further Notes

- The tool must never block a commit. It runs post-commit (or as a non-blocking pre-commit step). Exit code is always 0.
- SARIF file should be gitignored by default. Add a note in the docs.
- The `--json` output is the contract for agent consumption — treat it as a stable API from v1.0.

# TASKS.md — Implementation Slices

> Vertical slices, thin end-to-end. Each slice is independently completable and verifiable.
> Work top to bottom — each slice unblocks the next.

---

## Slice 1 — Skeleton + JUDGE.md loader

**Goal:** Bare project structure, installable CLI, JUDGE.md parsing works.

- `pyproject.toml` with `code-review` as entry point
- `cli.py` with Typer app, placeholder `run` command
- `judge.py` — `Judge` dataclass, `load_judges(path)` that reads all `judges/*/JUDGE.md`
- YAML frontmatter parsing (name, version, mode, timeout_seconds)
- Body extraction (everything after second `---`)
- 1 bundled judge: `judges/naming/JUDGE.md` (content can be a stub)

**Done when:** `pip install -e .` works, `code-review --help` prints, `load_judges()` returns a populated list.

---

## Slice 2 — LLM call + one judge end-to-end

**Goal:** One real judge runs on a real diff and returns a parsed score.

- `llm.py` — thin Anthropic SDK wrapper, `call(system, user, timeout)` → raw text
- `runner.py` — `run_judge(judge, diff)` → calls LLM, parses JSON response
- Error handling: non-JSON response → `JudgeError`, timeout → `JudgeTimeout`
- Hardcode the diff in a test script for now (no git integration yet)
- `naming` judge has a real prompt that actually works

**Done when:** Running the test script produces a valid `{"score": N, "reasoning": "...", "violations": [...]}` from the API.

---

## Slice 3 — Git diff extraction + `code-review run` (terminal output)

**Goal:** `code-review run` reads real git diff, runs all judges, prints Rich summary.

- `runner.py` — `get_diff(staged=False)` via `subprocess` + `git diff HEAD~1 HEAD`
- `--staged` flag → `git diff --cached`
- Run all judges concurrently via `asyncio.gather()`
- `output/rich_output.py` — summary table: icon, judge name, score bar, score/10
- Failing judges (score < 6.0) show top violation inline
- All 5 bundled judges loaded and running

**Done when:** After a real commit, `code-review run` prints a readable summary with real scores.

---

## Slice 4 — `--json` output flag

**Goal:** `code-review run --json` outputs structured JSON to stdout.

- `output/json_output.py` — serializes run results to stable JSON schema
- Schema: `{ summary: { overall, judges: [...] }, results: { <judge>: { score, violations, improvements } } }`
- `--json` flag suppresses Rich output entirely
- `.code-review-state.json` written after every run

**Done when:** `code-review run --json | jq .summary.overall` returns a number.

---

## Slice 5 — Progressive disclosure: `code-review show`

**Goal:** Agent can drill into specific judge findings.

- `code-review show <judge>` — lists all violations from last run (reads state file)
- `code-review show <judge> --issue <n>` — full detail for one issue
- Updates `.code-review-state.json` with `focus` field
- Rich formatting for human, `--json` flag for agent

**Done when:** After `code-review run`, agent can query `code-review show naming --json` and get structured issue list.

---

## Slice 6 — SARIF output

**Goal:** Every run writes a valid SARIF file for GitHub/GitLab annotations.

- `output/sarif.py` — builds SARIF 2.1.0 JSON from run results
- One `rule` per judge in `driver.rules`
- One `result` per violation, with `physicalLocation` (file + line)
- Written to `.code-review-report.sarif` after every run
- Add `.code-review-report.sarif` and `.code-review-state.json` to `.gitignore` template in docs

**Done when:** SARIF file validates against schema and GitHub Actions can consume it (manual test).

---

## Slice 7 — Polish + integration docs

**Goal:** Tool is ready to hand to another developer (or Claude Code session).

- `README.md` with install, usage, JUDGE.md format reference
- pre-commit integration snippet (copy-paste ready)
- husky integration snippet (copy-paste ready)
- `code-review run --help` is complete and accurate
- All 5 judges have real, tested prompts (not stubs)
- `pyproject.toml` has correct metadata for eventual PyPI publish

**Done when:** A fresh clone + `pip install -e .` + `code-review run` works with no extra configuration.

---

## Dependency order

```
Slice 1 → Slice 2 → Slice 3 → Slice 4
                              Slice 4 → Slice 5
                    Slice 3 → Slice 6
                    Slice 5 + Slice 6 → Slice 7
```

Slices 4, 5, 6 can be worked in parallel after Slice 3.

`judge` jako nazwa jest świetna — krótka, CLI-friendly, semantycznie idealna. `judge run` brzmi naturalnie, ale nawet sam `judge` jako default command bez subkomendy byłby elegancki.

Co do jury — masz rację że konotacja jest zła. Jury wydaje werdykt, nie ocenę. A cały sens tego systemu to właśnie granularne score'y, nie "guilty/not guilty".

Ale jest inne słowo z tego świata które pasuje lepiej: **bench**.

"The bench" to kolektyw sędziów jako ciało — ale bez zero-jedynkowej konotacji. "Panel" też działa. A najciekawsze jest to że `judge` i `bench` razem tworzą spójny słownik:

```
judge          ← CLI tool (czasownik i rzeczownik)
judge run      ← odpal panel
bench          ← zbiór załadowanych sędziów
judges/        ← katalog z JUDGE.md plikami
JUDGE.md       ← definicja sędziego
verdict        ← wynik całego runu (zamiast "report")
findings       ← lista issues od jednego sędziego (zamiast "violations")
```

Albo jeszcze prościej — zostać przy `judge` i nie nazywać zbioru osobno. "Your judges found 3 issues" jest naturalne bez potrzeby nazywania panelu.

Jedna praktyczna kwestia: sprawdź czy `judge` nie jest zajęty na PyPI zanim się przywiążesz do nazwy. Często trzeba dodać prefix — `judge-cli`, `judgecode`, coś w tym stylu.

Co do jury — masz rację że konotacja jest zła. Jury wydaje werdykt, nie ocenę. A cały sens tego systemu to właśnie granularne score'y, nie "guilty/not guilty".

Ale jest inne słowo z tego świata które pasuje lepiej: **bench**.

"The bench" to kolektyw sędziów jako ciało — ale bez zero-jedynkowej konotacji. "Panel" też działa. A najciekawsze jest to że `judge` i `bench` razem tworzą spójny słownik:

```
judge          ← CLI tool (czasownik i rzeczownik)
judge run      ← odpal panel
bench          ← zbiór załadowanych sędziów
judges/        ← katalog z JUDGE.md plikami
JUDGE.md       ← definicja sędziego
verdict        ← wynik całego runu (zamiast "report")
findings       ← lista issues od jednego sędziego (zamiast "violations")
```

Albo jeszcze prościej — zostać przy `judge` i nie nazywać zbioru osobno. "Your judges found 3 issues" jest naturalne bez potrzeby nazywania panelu.

Jedna praktyczna kwestia: sprawdź czy `judge` nie jest zajęty na PyPI zanim się przywiążesz do nazwy. Często trzeba dodać prefix — `judge-cli`, `judgecode`, coś w tym stylu.

The user is referring to SKILL.md files in Claude Code repositories. These are just markdown files that get dropped into a repo - no installation, no package manager, just a file. That's the key insight.

So the question "czy na pewno python?" is really asking: should we build judge as a Python CLI tool that needs to be installed, or should it be something simpler - like a collection of JUDGE.md files that Claude Code can pick up natively, with maybe a minimal runner?

Let me think about this. SKILL.md files:
- No installation needed
- Just copy/clone into your repo
- Claude Code reads them automatically
- Zero dependencies


- Work anywhere Claude Code works

The tension is that the user wants a standalone CLI tool for developers in the terminal, but also wants the simplicity of SKILL.md's distribution model - just drop files into a repo with no installation overhead. The real question becomes: how do we distribute the judge files themselves, and separately, what actually runs them?

A standalone binary in Go or Rust would best match SKILL.md's elegance - single file, no runtime dependencies, installable via brew or curl - but that requires building and maintaining a separate tool outside of Claude Code.To zmienia perspektywę fundamentalnie.

SKILL.md odnosi się sukcesem przez **zero install** — wrzucasz plik do repo i działa. Nie ma `pip install`, nie ma `npm install`, nie ma żadnego runtime. To jest właśnie dlaczego są popularne — friction jest praktycznie zerowy.

Jeśli chcesz się inspirować tym modelem, Python CLI jest **przeciwieństwem** tego podejścia. Wymaga: Python w PATH, `pip install`, virtual env, zależności.

Masz dwa oddzielne pytania:

**1. Dystrybucja judges (JUDGE.md)** — tu już masz SKILL.md model. Zero friction, wrzucasz plik, działa. ✅

**2. Dystrybucja runnera (CLI tool)** — tu jest problem. I masz kilka opcji:

| Runtime | Instalacja | Friction |
|---|---|---|
| Python | `pip install judge-cli` | Wysoki — wymaga Pythona |
| Node | `npx judge` | Średni — wymaga Node |
| **Go/Rust binary** | `brew install judge` lub `curl` | **Niski — jeden plik** |
| Wbudowany w Claude Code | Brak | **Zero — jak SKILL.md** |

---

### Najbliżej SKILL.md modelu

Standalone binary (Go lub Rust) — jeden plik wykonywalny, działa na każdym systemie bez żadnego runtime. Tak działa `gh`, `rg`, `fd`, `bat`. Instalacja to jeden `brew install` lub pobranie binarki.

Albo — najbardziej radykalna opcja — **runner jest Claude Code**. JUDGE.md to instrukcja którą Claude Code wykonuje bezpośrednio, bez osobnego narzędzia. Wtedy distribution model jest identyczny jak SKILL.md.

Które podejście Cię bardziej ciągnie?

**B.** `judge` jako skill w ekosystemie skills.sh — agent go wywołuje, nie człowiek bezpośrednio
**C.** Hybrydowo — JUDGE.md jako format, runner jako skill który można zainstalować przez `npx skills add`

Co o tym myślisz?
