# Documentation

Learn how to discover, install, and use skills with your AI agents.

The `skills` CLI that powers this leaderboard is open source at [github.com/vercel-labs/skills](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills).

## What are skills?

Skills are reusable capabilities for AI agents. They provide procedural knowledge that helps agents accomplish specific tasks more effectively. Think of them as plugins or extensions that enhance what your AI agent can do.

## Getting started

To install a skill, use the `skills` CLI:

```
npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills
```

This will install the skill and make it available to your AI agent.

## How skills are ranked

The skills leaderboard ranks skills based on anonymous telemetry data collected from the `skills` CLI. When users install skills, aggregated usage data helps surface the most popular and useful skills in the ecosystem.

This telemetry is completely anonymous and only tracks which skills are being installed—no personal information or usage patterns are collected.

## Browse skills

Visit the [homepage](/) to browse the skills leaderboard and discover new capabilities for your agents.

## How are you securing skills?

There are routine security audits that assess skills and their contents for malicious content. To report security issues, please visit [security.vercel.com](https://security.vercel.com/).

We do our best to maintain a safe ecosystem, but we cannot guarantee the quality or security of every skill listed on skills.sh. We encourage you to review skills before installing and use your own judgment.

# Judge — Feature List

> Version: 3.0
> Last updated: 2026-03-18
> Changelog: Renamed from "AI Code Review Framework". Added distribution architecture, zero-friction philosophy, npx judges ecosystem, skill integration. Removed Python-specific tooling references (TBD pending language decision).

---

## Core

- Git diff as the universal input unit
- Judges as plug-and-play units, each defined by a `JUDGE.md` file
- `JUDGE.md` uses YAML frontmatter (same convention as `SKILL.md`)
- Each judge evaluates exactly one aspect of the code, scored 0–10
- Per-judge score + aggregate overall score
- SARIF as the standard output format (compatible with GitHub, GitLab, VS Code)

---

## Judge Definition (JUDGE.md)

- YAML frontmatter: `name`, `version`, `mode`, `tools`, `max_tool_calls`, `timeout_seconds`
- Body: the judge's system prompt
- Three execution modes per judge:
  - `one-shot` — single LLM call, diff only
  - `agent` — multi-step, can explore repo via tools
  - `auto` — judge decides whether diff is sufficient or deeper exploration is needed
- Agent-mode tools (configurable per judge): `read_file`, `search_symbol`, `grep`, and others
- Hard limits: `max_tool_calls` and `timeout_seconds` per judge invocation

---

## Judge Types

- **One-shot judges** — operate purely on the diff (e.g. naming, magic numbers, no-comments)
- **Agent judges** — use diff as entry point, explore repo for big-picture context (e.g. SRP, architecture)
- Agent judges can suggest changes outside the files in the diff
- Agent judges leave execution traces (files visited, patterns found) for observability

---

## Distribution — zero friction philosophy

Strongly inspired by the `skills.sh` / `npx skills` ecosystem (Vercel Labs, open-source).

Core principle: **installing a judge should be as easy as copying a file.**

- `JUDGE.md` is the atomic unit — language-agnostic, shareable, no runtime required
- Installation scopes:
  - `~/.judge/judges/` — global (all projects)
  - `./.judge/judges/` — per project (local, committed to repo)
- Local scope overrides global (same precedence model as gitconfig)
- Manual install: copy `JUDGE.md` to the right folder — always works
- CLI install: `npx judges add owner/repo` — thin wrapper, pulls from GitHub (mirrors `npx skills add`)
- Runner (`judge` CLI) is a separate concern from judge distribution

---

## Judges Ecosystem

- Each judge is independent and interchangeable
- A judge may internally use other skills
- Judges can be composed into named packs (e.g. "Uncle Bob pack", "Security pack")
- Community ecosystem modeled on skills.sh — GitHub as the registry, no central server
- Community quality signal via stars/usage, not mandatory benchmarking

---

## CLI Interface (`judge`)

- Standalone usage — single command, no setup required
- Progressive disclosure — summary first, details on demand
- Queryable by judge, by issue, by file
- `--json` output flag for agent consumption
- Human-readable terminal output
- Per-session judge reprioritization (developer or agent can promote/demote judges)

---

## Skills Integration

- A companion skill (`judge-skill`) teaches AI agents how to use the `judge` CLI
- Installable via `npx skills add owner/judge-skill`
- Follows identical distribution model to any other skill in the skills.sh ecosystem

---

## Git Hook Integrations

- **pre-commit** (Python ecosystem) — via local hook definition
- **husky** (JS/TS ecosystem) — via `.husky/` shell script
- One-command setup snippets provided for each
- Tool itself has no opinion on hook runner — it's just a CLI

---

## CI/CD

- GitLab CI integration
- GitHub Actions integration
- SARIF output → native PR annotations (GitHub, GitLab)

---

## Dashboard

- Live view of all judge scores for the current session
- Agent activity tracking via CLI call observation
- Score history across commits (trend per judge)

---

## Budget Controls

- Per-judge `max_tool_calls` limit (agent mode)
- Per-judge `timeout_seconds` limit
- Future: global cost budget per run

---

## LLM Backend

- PoC: Anthropic SDK (Claude)
- Future: vendor-agnostic via LiteLLM or equivalent

---

## General

> Version: 3.0
> Last updated: 2026-03-18
> Changelog: Renamed from "AI Code Review Framework". Added distribution architecture, zero-friction philosophy, npx judges ecosystem, skill integration. Removed Python-specific tooling references (TBD pending language decision).

---

## Core

- Git diff as the universal input unit
- Judges as plug-and-play units, each defined by a `JUDGE.md` file
- `JUDGE.md` uses YAML frontmatter (same convention as `SKILL.md`)
- Each judge evaluates exactly one aspect of the code, scored 0–10
- Per-judge score + aggregate overall score
- SARIF as the standard output format (compatible with GitHub, GitLab, VS Code)

---

## Judge Definition (JUDGE.md)

- YAML frontmatter: `name`, `version`, `mode`, `tools`, `max_tool_calls`, `timeout_seconds`
- Body: the judge's system prompt
- Three execution modes per judge:
  - `one-shot` — single LLM call, diff only
  - `agent` — multi-step, can explore repo via tools
  - `auto` — judge decides whether diff is sufficient or deeper exploration is needed
- Agent-mode tools (configurable per judge): `read_file`, `search_symbol`, `grep`, and others
- Hard limits: `max_tool_calls` and `timeout_seconds` per judge invocation

---

## Judge Types

- **One-shot judges** — operate purely on the diff (e.g. naming, magic numbers, no-comments)
- **Agent judges** — use diff as entry point, explore repo for big-picture context (e.g. SRP, architecture)
- Agent judges can suggest changes outside the files in the diff
- Agent judges leave execution traces (files visited, patterns found) for observability

---

Strongly inspired by the `skills.sh` / `npx skills` ecosystem (Vercel Labs, open-source).

Core principle: **installing a judge should be as easy as copying a file.**

- `JUDGE.md` is the atomic unit — language-agnostic, shareable, no runtime required
- Installation scopes:
  - `~/.judge/judges/` — global (all projects)
  - `./.judge/judges/` — per project (local, committed to repo)
- Local scope overrides global (same precedence model as gitconfig)
- Manual install: copy `JUDGE.md` to the right folder — always works
- CLI install: `npx judges add owner/repo` — thin wrapper, pulls from GitHub (mirrors `npx skills add`)
- Runner (`judge` CLI) is a separate concern from judge distribution

---

## Judges Ecosystem

- Each judge is independent and interchangeable
- A judge may internally use other skills
- Judges can be composed into named packs (e.g. "Uncle Bob pack", "Security pack")
- Community ecosystem modeled on skills.sh — GitHub as the registry, no central server
- Community quality signal via stars/usage, not mandatory benchmarking

---

## CLI Interface (`judge`)

- Standalone usage — single command, no setup required
- Progressive disclosure — summary first, details on demand
- Queryable by judge, by issue, by file
- `--json` output flag for agent consumption
- Human-readable terminal output
- Per-session judge reprioritization (developer or agent can promote/demote judges)

---

- A companion skill (`judge-skill`) teaches AI agents how to use the `judge` CLI
- Installable via `npx skills add owner/judge-skill`
- Follows identical distribution model to any other skill in the skills.sh ecosystem

---

- **pre-commit** (Python ecosystem) — via local hook definition
- **husky** (JS/TS ecosystem) — via `.husky/` shell script
- One-command setup snippets provided for each

- GitLab CI integration
- GitHub Actions integration
- SARIF output → native PR annotations (GitHub, GitLab)

---

- Live view of all judge scores for the current session
- Agent activity tracking via CLI call observation
- Score history across commits (trend per judge)

- Per-judge `timeout_seconds` limit
- Future: global cost budget per run

- PoC: Anthropic SDK (Claude)
- Future: vendor-agnostic via LiteLLM or equivalent

## General

# Feature: Input Modes

> Status: Draft v0.1
> Last updated: 2026-03-18

---

## Summary

`judge` accepts code input in two modes: **diff mode** and **file mode**. Git is not required. The tool behaves like a linter — it takes paths or streams as input and doesn't care where they come from.

---

## Modes

### Diff mode

Evaluates what changed. Entry point for the standard commit workflow.

```bash
judge diff                        # last commit (git diff HEAD~1 HEAD)
judge diff --staged               # staged files (git diff --cached)
judge diff HEAD~3                 # last 3 commits
judge diff main..feature-branch   # branch comparison
git diff | judge diff --stdin     # piped diff
```

**What a judge receives in this mode:**
- The raw unified diff (which lines changed, added, removed)
- Full current content of every file that appears in the diff

The judge sees *what changed* and *what the file looks like now*. This allows evaluating a renamed variable in context of the whole function, or checking SRP with the full class visible — not just the changed lines.

### File mode

Evaluates files or directories directly. No git required.

```bash
judge README.md                   # single file
judge src/scrapers/               # directory (recursive)
judge .                           # entire project
judge src/**/*.ts                 # glob
```

**What a judge receives in this mode:**
- Full content of each matched file
- No diff — the entire file is the input

Useful for: onboarding a legacy codebase, reviewing a PR without git access, running in CI on changed files passed explicitly.

---

## Input contract (per judge call)

Regardless of mode, a judge always receives a single structured input:

```json
{
  "mode": "diff",
  "diff": "--- a/src/scraper.py\n+++ b/src/scraper.py\n...",
  "files": [
    {
      "path": "src/scraper.py",
      "content": "... full file content ..."
    }
  ]
}
```

In file mode, `diff` is `null`. In diff mode, both are present.

---

## One call per judge, all files together

All changed/matched files are sent in a **single LLM call per judge** — not one call per file.

**Why:** Cross-file context matters. A judge evaluating naming conventions should see that `user_id` is used in one file and `userId` in another. A per-file call would miss this entirely.

**Trade-off:** Larger prompts = higher cost and latency. Acceptable for PoC. Future optimisation: chunking strategy for very large diffs, or a `--per-file` flag for lightweight runs.

---

## Default behaviour (no arguments)

```bash
judge        # in a git repo:     equivalent to `judge diff --staged`
             # outside a git repo: error, suggest `judge .` or `judge <path>`
```

---

## Compatibility with hook runners

Since `judge` is just a CLI that accepts paths and flags, hook runners pass input to it the same way they pass it to any linter:

**pre-commit:**
```yaml
- id: judge
  entry: judge diff --staged
  pass_filenames: false
```

**husky:**
```bash
# .husky/post-commit
judge diff
```

**lint-staged** (file mode, for per-file workflows):
```json
{
  "*.ts": "judge"
}
```

---

## Out of scope for this feature

- Diff mode for non-git VCS (svn, mercurial)
- Remote diffs (GitHub PR API, GitLab MR API) — future
- Binary files — always skipped, never sent to judges

## Input contract (runner → LLM)

`JUDGE.md` is a passive definition — a system prompt and config. It does not "receive" input. The **runner** is the actor that orchestrates the call.

For each judge, the runner:
1. Reads `JUDGE.md` — extracts system prompt and config
2. Builds a formatted text prompt from the input data
3. Sends `system prompt (from JUDGE.md)` + `formatted input` to the LLM
4. Parses the response into a structured result

The formatted input sent to the LLM looks like this (plain text, not JSON):

```
## DIFF
--- a/src/scraper.py
+++ b/src/scraper.py
@@ -12,7 +12,7 @@
-def process(d):
+def process(data):
...

## FILE: src/scraper.py
(full file content)

## FILE: src/utils.py
(full file content)
```

In file mode, the `DIFF` section is omitted. `JUDGE.md` never sees raw JSON — it always receives readable, structured text. The runner owns the formatting decision.

input.file_text:
# Feature: Ignore Rules

> Status: Problem definition — no solution decided
> Last updated: 2026-03-18

---

## Problem

A judge may flag something the developer intentionally accepts — a legacy class name that's too expensive to rename, a magic number that's actually a well-known constant, an architectural pattern that violates a rule but is correct for the context.

The developer needs a way to say: **"I know, and I don't want to hear about this again."**

---

## Why this is hard

Judge output is **non-deterministic**. The same piece of code evaluated twice may produce:

- Different phrasing of the same finding
- Different line numbers if surrounding code shifted
- Different symbol names if the judge describes it differently
- A finding that disappears and reappears across runs

This makes it impossible to match a suppression rule against a specific past finding reliably.

---

## Approaches considered (not decided)

### By file path / glob
Suppress all findings from a judge for a given path.
```
# .judgeignore
src/legacy/**
src/generated/**
```
- Simple, deterministic, easy to maintain
- Too coarse — suppresses everything for a judge in that path

### By file + symbol
Suppress a finding for a specific named symbol in a specific file.
```yaml
- judge: naming
  file: src/legacy/processor.py
  symbol: UserDataProcessor
```
- More precise
- Language-specific — "symbol" means different things in Python, TS, Go
- Maintenance burden: symbol names change, files move
- Requires judges to consistently report symbol names in their output (contract dependency)

### By inline annotation
Suppress via a comment in the source file itself (like `eslint-disable`).
```python
class UserDataProcessor:  # judge-ignore: naming
```
- Developer intent is co-located with code
- Works across renames and file moves
- Pollutes source code with tooling annotations
- Not all file types support comments

### By fingerprint
Hash the finding (file + rough location + violation type) and store suppressed hashes.
- Attempts to survive minor reformatting
- Fragile — any change to judge prompt changes fingerprints
- Hard to audit ("what did I suppress and why?")

---

## Open questions

- Should suppressions be committed to the repo (team-wide) or local only (personal)?
- Should a suppressed finding still appear in output, but marked as "suppressed"? Or silently hidden?
- How does this interact with agent mode — should the agent be aware of suppressions?
- Is `.judgeignore` (path-based) sufficient for 80% of cases, and finer-grained suppression a v2 problem?

---

## Related

- Feature: Judge weights (separate doc — a softer version of the same problem)
- SARIF has a native `suppress` mechanism — worth investigating as a standard

chat_messages.text:
Bez zastanowienia: **prompt engineering dla sędziów**.

Nie dlatego że jest technicznie skomplikowany — kod runnera jest prosty. Ale dlatego że to jedyne miejsce gdzie nie możesz się mylić i szybko naprawić.

Konkretnie chodzi o kontrakt outputu. Każdy sędzia musi zwrócić JSON który runner sparsuje:

```json
{
  "score": 4.8,
  "reasoning": "...",
  "violations": [...],
  "improvements": [...]
}
```

Problem: LLM jest niedeterministyczny. Czasem zwróci markdown wokół JSONa. Czasem zagnieździ inaczej. Czasem score będzie stringiem zamiast liczbą. Czasem przy trudnym diffie "zapomni" o formacie i zacznie tłumaczyć prozą.

I to się mnoży przez liczbę sędziów — każdy ma nieco inny prompt, każdy może failować inaczej.

---

Drugie najtrudniejsze: **obsługa błędów w sposób który nie psuje UX**. Jeśli jeden sędzia timeout'uje albo zwróci śmieć, pozostałe cztery powinny się pokazać normalnie. To wymaga dobrego error boundary per judge, żeby jeden failure nie wysypał całego runu.

---

Reszta — CLI, SARIF, formatowanie outputu, ładowanie JUDGE.md — to jest mechanika. Nudna, ale przewidywalna.

Dlatego zaczęłbym PoC od napisania jednego sędziego i odpalania go ręcznie na kilku różnych diffach, zanim napiszę cokolwiek innego. Żeby wiedzieć jak prompt się zachowuje zanim zbuduję runner który na nim polega.

---
Hej Claude,
chcę, żebyś od razu przyjął nową zasadę projektową i przestał w ogóle myśleć w kategoriach „score 0-10 per judge”. To nie jest dyskusja — to decyzja produktowa po analizie feedbacku od GPT i mojej własnej refleksji. Od teraz projektujemy **findings-first**, a nie scores.
### Dlaczego scoring 0-10 jest słaby i zły pomysł
1. **Fałszywa precyzja**  
   LLM nie jest w stanie konsekwentnie odróżnić 6.7 od 6.8. Różnica między runami na tym samym diffie potrafi wynosić ±1.5–2.0 punktu. Użytkownik zobaczy „Architecture: 6.7/10” i uzna to za obiektywny pomiar — a to jest tylko uporządkowana opinia modelu. To klasyczny problem LLM-as-judge, który Anthropic i Promptfoo otwarcie nazywają pułapką.
2. **Zabija zaufanie**  
   Albo użytkownicy przestaną ufać narzędziu („znowu mi dał 5.9, nie wiem dlaczego”), albo zaufają za bardzo i będą traktować liczby jak świętość. W obu przypadkach produkt traci sens.
3. **Komplikuje wszystko inne**  
   - Suppress/ignore staje się koszmarem (jak zignorować „6.7”?).  
   - CI/CD thresholds są bez sensu.  
   - Agent mode nie wie, co zrobić z liczbą.  
   - Kalibracja jest prawie niemożliwa.
4. **Nie daje wartości, której dev naprawdę potrzebuje**  
   Dev nie chce „średniej 6.4”. Chce wiedzieć:  
   - co jest naprawdę źle,  
   - jak bardzo źle (high/medium/low),  
   - jak bardzo jestem pewien,  
   - i co konkretnie zrobić.
### Co zamiast tego proponuję (nowy model – od razu wdrażaj)
**Per finding** (to jest serce outputu):
```json
{
  "rule_id": "naming:too-generic-variable",
  "instance": "res",
  "severity": "medium",           // high | medium | low
  "confidence": "high",           // high | medium | low
  "message": "nazwa zmiennej `res` jest zbyt ogólna",
  "location": "src/scrapers/steam_scraper.py:47",
  "fix_hint": "rozważ filtered_products lub steam_products"
}
```
**Na poziomie judge’a:**
- Liczba findings: `2 high, 1 medium`
- Status: `needs attention` / `good` / `excellent`
**Na poziomie `judge diff`:**
```
naming              ⚠  3 medium
magic-numbers       ✗  2 high
→ needs attention (2 high issues total)
```
Zero liczb 0-10 nigdzie na froncie. Tylko czytelne kategorie jak w Ruff/ESLint/Semgrep.
### Dodatkowe konsekwencje (wdrożone od razu)
- W JUDGE.md musi być sekcja **Output contract** z `rule_id` + `instance`.
- `.judgeignore` działa na `rule_id` i `rule_id:instance`.
- Inline suppression: `# judge-ignore: naming:too-generic-variable`
- W CLI pokazujemy findings + suppress info, a nie średnie.
Chcę, żebyś teraz:
1. Przerobił wszystkie istniejące JUDGE.md na nowy kontrakt.
2. Zaktualizował runner i CLI mockup.
3. Dodał do feature-ignore-rules.md sekcję „Proposed solution v1: rule_id + instance”.
Od tej chwili każdy twój pomysł ma zaczynać się od „findings + severity + confidence”, a nie od „score 0-10”. Jasne?
Daj znać, jak rozumiesz i ruszamy z implementacją.
--- 
Wklej to w całości — jest gotowe do użycia.
